video_title: The Rise of Organized Retail Crime at Big Box Stores | Odd Lots
gist: Home Depot's VP of asset protection Scott Glenn walks Odd Lots through the economics of retail shrink: how the company splits ~30% operational vs. ~70% malicious loss, why one $799 drill kit was stolen 4.2 times for every unit sold, why RFID and camera-based detection still fail the capex test in a 140,000-square-foot steel-framed store, and how stolen goods now flow to peer-to-peer marketplaces exempted by a loophole in the 2023 INFORM Consumers Act. He argues organized retail crime is under-reported post-COVID and is bullish that the pending Combating Organized Retail Crime Act — passed by the House and attached to the NDAA — will finally put federal prosecutors and resources behind a crime that is inherently interstate.

insights.claim: Home Depot splits shrink into operational/administrative loss (roughly 30% of the total, 'things we do to ourself') versus malicious loss (the remaining ~70%, 'things people do to us'), and reports it separately across three channels: supply chain, retail stores, and online.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: When a retailer blames a shrink miss on 'theft,' this split is the diagnostic question — a rising operational component signals inventory-control and process failure, which is a management problem, not a crime problem.
insights.quote: about 30% of our strength is falls into that operational administrative things we do to ourself type of of category. And then the balance of it falls into more of the malicious side

insights.claim: Cross-retailer shrink comparisons are close to meaningless because companies categorize operational versus administrative versus malicious shrink differently, and because some retailers use retail accounting while others use cost accounting.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Treat headline shrink-rate comparisons between retailers as non-comparable; only intra-company year-over-year trends and management's own bridge are usable signal.
insights.quote: how people categorize shrink what somebody calls operational shrink versus administrative versus malicious can vary by retailers

insights.claim: The long-standing industry rule of thumb is that roughly 40% of malicious shrink is caused by a retailer's own employees and about 35% by outsiders walking into stores, with the balance self-inflicted operational and administrative loss.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Internal theft is the largest single bucket, meaning labor-model changes, turnover and store staffing levels are as much a shrink variable as street crime — relevant when retailers cut hours to protect margin.
insights.quote: 40% of shrink on the malicious side is done by associates working for the company. They cause 40% of your loss, 35% are people walking into your store

insights.claim: Home Depot's asset protection lead believes organized retail crime losses have been drifting up and have been systematically under-reported since COVID, so police reports and FBI uniform crime statistics understate the true level.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: The widely cited skeptic argument that official crime stats show no shoplifting surge may be measuring reporting behavior rather than crime; expect continued divergence between company shrink disclosures and public crime data.
insights.quote: I believe they're starting to drift up. And I also believe since Covid, they've been underreported.

insights.claim: The largest share of Home Depot's shrink occurs in its roughly 2,300–2,400 retail stores rather than in distribution or online channels.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Store-level intervention (lockups, staffing, edge video) still drives most of the recoverable shrink dollars, so capex aimed at stores — not the supply chain — is where a shrink-reduction program shows up first in gross margin.

insights.claim: An executive who arrived at Home Depot in 2018 says he was not initially a believer in organized retail crime as a distinct problem and only became convinced as post-COVID omnichannel resale made impersonal, anonymous liquidation of stolen goods easy.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: The causal driver is resale liquidity, not just policing — meaning marketplace regulation and platform behavior are the real levers on shrink, more than store security spending.
insights.quote: I have become a believer in one organized retail crime exists. It's become more lucrative, it's become more pervasive. Um, and it's become more dangerous

insights.claim: Home Depot found one combination power-tool kit priced at $799 that it had to buy 4.2 times for every single unit it actually sold, making the SKU's gross margin mix structurally negative before any security intervention.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: This is the concrete arithmetic that justifies lockups to a CFO: a single high-theft SKU can consume more than four units of COGS per unit of revenue, so lockup decisions are gross-margin arbitrage, not theater.
insights.quote: one particular combination of kit that we were selling for $799, we would buy it 4.2 times for every time we sell it

insights.claim: Locking up merchandise does not reliably reduce sales, and in many categories sales actually rise after lockup because the product is finally in stock when customers arrive.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the consensus that lockups destroy conversion; for retailers with high-theft SKUs, lockups can be net revenue-accretive via in-stock rates, which reframes them as a margin and availability play rather than pure cost.
insights.quote: there's also many, many categories were actually sales go up because you're in stock

insights.claim: Home Depot uses QR codes on its lockups that summon an associate via phone, with an average unlock time of about 90 seconds, and is exploring letting verified pro-loyalty members self-service the cases.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Ninety seconds is the benchmark to measure any retailer's lockup friction against; loyalty-gated self-service turns anti-theft hardware into a loyalty-enrollment funnel, an underappreciated data-capture angle.
insights.quote: we use QR codes on all of our lock ups that summon somebody through our, our phone that they come and it takes on average about 90s for that, that lock up to be unlocked by person

insights.claim: Out-of-stocks caused by theft carry outsized cost at Home Depot because pros and contractors — stated in the interview as 50% and elsewhere as 58% of revenue — leave an active job site to buy a replacement tool and cannot tolerate a failed trip.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: For pro-weighted retailers, shrink's real cost is lost pro loyalty and trip failure, not the stolen unit — so shrink is a revenue-retention KPI, and pro mix raises the return on anti-theft investment.
insights.quote: we're in a business that 58% of our revenue comes from pros and contractors. If they leave a job site uh, to to because their drill broke and they go to the store because it said we had one and we don't, that's a problem too

insights.claim: Retailers decide what to lock up through an arduous, data-driven negotiation with merchants and operators over a curated SKU list, rather than blanket-locking categories, and the internal target for shrink is zero while the achievable number is 'somewhere north of that.'
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Watch for retailers that lock up broadly rather than surgically — it signals they lack the SKU-level loss data to make the trade-off, and it is a proxy for weaker inventory analytics.

insights.claim: Blanket camera coverage of a 140,000-square-foot Home Depot store is economically prohibitive because of hardware and processing costs, so full computer-vision theft detection exists only in selected aisles rather than store-wide.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Store-wide AI theft detection is a capex story, not a software story — the bottleneck is camera density and compute, which favors vendors selling edge inference on existing cameras over those requiring new installs.
insights.quote: But it is expensive and it's a it's a lot of processing power. It's a lot of hardware that you have to put into your stores.

insights.claim: Passive RFID does not work inside Home Depot stores because the steel inventory effectively creates a Faraday cage, forcing a move to more expensive active pinging RFID.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A physics constraint, not a cost curve, blocks RFID in hardware/home-improvement formats — so RFID adoption stories that work for apparel retailers should not be extrapolated to big-box hardware.
insights.quote: We are a hardware store with a basically a Faraday cage of, you know, steal throughout our stores. We do a passive RFID does not work in our stores.

insights.claim: RFID tag costs are now effectively nil; the remaining barrier is the in-store reader hardware needed for full coverage, made worse in Home Depot's case by eight separate store entrances.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: The investable part of the RFID chain has shifted from tag manufacturers to reader/infrastructure vendors; any supplier that collapses reader cost unlocks a large latent big-box retrofit market.
insights.quote: tag costs are nil at this point. That's not really the issue. It is truly the hardware capabilities to be able to put it everywhere.

insights.claim: Home Depot tested embedding Bluetooth-style chips directly into products ('bricking') but found it very hard to scale because it would require re-engineering an entire supplier production line, such as a Milwaukee drill line, against thin category margins.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Source-tagging and product-bricking solutions require vendor-side manufacturing change, so adoption depends on tool OEMs, not retailers — a slower, supplier-gated timeline than security-tech marketing implies.

insights.claim: Home Depot has just replaced its video management system across all its stores to enable edge analytics on existing cameras, flagging behaviors like lingering, avoiding associates, or entering restricted areas rather than identifying theft acts directly.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A completed fleet-wide VMS refresh at 2,300+ stores is a concrete, recent spend — evidence that the near-term retail-security TAM is edge inference retrofits on installed camera bases.
insights.quote: we just replaced our entire video analytics, um, our video management system in all 2300 stores, uh, to, to an upgraded version that allows us to now put edge analytics on our cameras

insights.claim: Home Depot's typical organized-retail-crime case takes about 70 days from discovery to handoff to police, and the company has more cases than it can investigate, so AI is being deployed as a cycle-time compression play rather than a detection breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: The ROI framing for AI in loss prevention is investigator throughput per headcount, not accuracy — the same efficiency argument that governs AI adoption in legal, claims and fraud operations.
insights.quote: our typical O'Rourke case takes about 70 days from discovery to closure to handing off to the police department. Um, and so if we can compress that time frame, we can turn more.

insights.claim: Retail security technology is ultimately capped by liability, not detection: staff are trained to de-escalate and back away rather than stop thieves, because Home Depot has had associates injured and killed in theft incidents.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Better detection alone cannot reduce shrink if interdiction is forbidden — value accrues to prosecution-enabling evidence and marketplace enforcement, not to in-store alarms.
insights.quote: I'll trade the shrink for the safety of the people every day of the week.

insights.claim: The organized retail crime supply chain runs boosters (recruited thieves paid in cash or drugs and given shopping lists) to fences who strip tags and identifying stickers and relist the product, with proceeds kicked up to organizers who may be cartels or transnational gangs.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Understanding the three-layer structure explains why arresting shoplifters does nothing to shrink rates — the economics only break when the fence's resale channel or the payment rails are disrupted.

insights.claim: Stolen resale prices track how technology-laden the item is: internet-connected and tech products plus gift cards clear at roughly 70–80% of retail, while commodity consumables like deodorant, t-shirts and Tylenol clear at only 30–40 cents on the dollar.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Recovery value determines which SKUs attract organized theft, so retailers with high tech-content assortments carry structurally higher malicious shrink risk than consumables retailers at equal footprint.
insights.quote: if it's internet connected, it sells very, very close to retail

insights.claim: The 2023 INFORM Consumers Act pushed stolen-goods resale off large marketplaces like Amazon and eBay by forcing seller verification, but a loophole left peer-to-peer platforms such as Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist uncovered, and volume migrated there.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A clear regulatory-arbitrage map: if Congress closes the peer-to-peer loophole, Meta and other P2P platforms absorb meaningful new compliance and know-your-seller cost that Amazon and eBay already carry.
insights.quote: there was a loophole in that bill that did not cover the peer to peer resellers. Um, can't explain why happened. Just it happened.

insights.claim: Home Depot runs its own marketplace-crawling models that flag sellers listing new-in-box products below Home Depot's own cost, and many investigations now start on the marketplace and work backwards to the store rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Below-cost new-in-box listing velocity is a usable public signal of a retailer's theft exposure, and a data source an analyst could scrape independently of company disclosure.
insights.quote: if Home Depot sells this com combination drill kit for $499, how in the heck is, you know, Tommy 1234 selling it for 200

insights.claim: Home Depot's asset protection lead says he is both disappointed and surprised that large peer-to-peer platforms make retailers do the detection work, arguing platforms should suspend sellers who systematically undercut retail cost rather than waiting to be told.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A large retailer publicly pressing platforms on stolen-goods enforcement raises the odds of both legislation and reputational campaigns aimed at Meta's marketplace business.
insights.quote: It seems a little backwards to me that I should have to come and tell them that they've got somebody selling stolen product on their site

insights.claim: Supply-chain theft splits into three modes: outright diversion of full trailer loads at ports and transport facilities, physical break-ins to parked trailers while drivers sleep, and fraudulent pickups using fake bills of lading and forged paperwork.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Each mode has a different mitigation and a different vendor — electronic BOL and carrier-identity verification address the fastest-growing mode, which is paperwork fraud rather than physical break-in.

insights.claim: AI is being used by criminals to forge convincing pickup paperwork, so what is new in cargo theft is the volume of fraudulent-pickup attempts rather than the scheme itself; electronic billing is the countermeasure being adopted.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Generative AI is lowering the cost of documentary fraud across logistics — a tailwind for digital freight documentation, carrier-vetting and identity-verification providers in the freight stack.
insights.quote: I is playing a space in this where they're able to kind of duplicate some of the some of the, um, uh, you know, capacities that allow a driver to walk, just drive straight in and say, I'm here to pick up trailer one, two, three, four, five

insights.claim: Rail theft has grown materially over the past five or six years, with mobs stripping parked railcars in yards and along unused 'dead track,' and the thieves show selective targeting that implies insider information from shipping and trucking companies.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Selective targeting implies insider leakage of manifest data, which makes rail-yard security and shipment-data access controls a rising cost line for Class I railroads and their high-value shippers.
insights.quote: they don't hit every trailer or every car on the rail. They hit the car on the rail that has the product that they really want to go after.

insights.claim: Online and omnichannel shrink is dominated by payments fraud — credit card and gift card fraud — plus a return-fraud loop where buyers extract and keep the product, return a substituted item, and collect a full refund.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: E-commerce shrink is a payments and returns-authorization problem, which routes the spend toward fraud-detection and returns-management software rather than physical security.

insights.claim: The Combating Organized Retail Crime Act has passed the House, been attached to the NDAA, and awaits Senate passage with the President having indicated he will sign — it would be the first federal organized-retail-crime statute providing dedicated prosecutors, coordination centers and amendments to the federal stolen-goods code.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A near-term, NDAA-attached legislative catalyst that bundles cargo theft, gift-card and payments fraud into one bill — a watchable event for retail shrink guidance and for marketplace compliance costs.
insights.quote: This is like literally the first organized retail crime Act at the federal level that provides resources. Prosecutors. Coordination centers.

insights.claim: Organized retail crime is structurally a federal problem because goods cross state lines, yet until now there have been no dedicated federal resources assigned to interstate transportation of stolen retail goods.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Explains why local policing metrics have not moved shrink — the enforcement gap is jurisdictional, so federal resourcing is the variable that could actually change loss rates.

insights.claim: Political momentum has reversed sharply: 35 states now run attorney-general-led organized retail crime task forces across both parties, with 100–200-plus bipartisan House sponsors of CORCA, versus a decriminalization and defund-the-police climate seven years ago.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Bipartisan breadth makes this one of the more durable regulatory trends in retail — supportive for loss-prevention vendors and a persistent cost overhang for resale marketplaces.
insights.quote: seven years ago, I was doom and gloom on this like nobody was taking this seriously.

insights.claim: Retailers are effectively subsidizing public law enforcement by delivering cases roughly 80% complete, because under-resourced police departments triage retail theft below violent crime and will only take cases where the investigative work is already done.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Private investigative capacity is now a required retail operating expense; any retailer without a professional ORC investigations unit has structurally lower recovery and deterrence.
insights.quote: Our job is to hand them a case file that is 80% complete

insights.claim: Home Depot staffs its Atlanta organized-retail-crime unit largely with former federal, state and local law enforcement agents who stitch local store incidents into multi-store cases using video analytics and vehicle and identity matching.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: Corporate loss prevention is absorbing ex-law-enforcement talent at scale — a structural labor-cost trend in retail SG&A that scales with store count.

insights.claim: Loyalty-app-unlocked merchandise cases would solve lockup friction but effectively create an identity system for physical shopping, tying the ability to buy certain goods to enrollment in a retailer's identity graph.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway, co-host
insights.so_what: Anti-theft hardware becomes a customer-data acquisition channel, strengthening first-party retail data assets and retail media businesses as a side effect of shrink control.
insights.quote: you're kind of getting close to an almost identity system for shopping

insights.claim: Once edge AI can run behavioral suspicion models on cameras already installed in stores, deployment becomes inevitable regardless of public objection, because the technology rather than policy drives adoption.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal, co-host
insights.so_what: Implies a secular demand floor for in-store behavioral analytics vendors and a rising regulatory/privacy-backlash risk to retailers that deploy them first.
insights.quote: if you could just have a model embedded onto the camera itself that could just say, identify suspicious behavior in real time, it will be implemented

insights.claim: Detection technology without the ability to interdict only shifts the bottleneck to police willingness to prosecute, so surveillance spending may not convert into lower shrink.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway, co-host
insights.so_what: A skeptic's check on the loss-prevention-tech investment case: without CORCA-style prosecution capacity, security capex may not show up in shrink improvement.

insights.claim: Crime is displacement-resistant across retail formats: as physical shoplifting is suppressed it migrates into online payments and returns fraud, and any future automated defense such as security robots will itself spawn new attack surfaces.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal, co-host
insights.so_what: Shrink is a permanent operating cost that changes form rather than disappearing, so model it as a structural margin drag across channel shifts rather than a fixable one-off.
insights.quote: the crime finds a way and new forms of crime will emerge

insights.claim: Copper and wire are the highest-dollar theft categories at Home Depot and theft volume tracks the copper price, with a rise in the commodity making it materially more attractive to thieves.
insights.speaker: Scott Glenn, VP of asset protection, The Home Depot
insights.so_what: A direct, tradable linkage: sustained high copper prices raise metals-theft loss for home-improvement retailers, utilities and construction — a shrink cost that is effectively a short position in the copper price.
insights.quote: it is, uh, definitely a commodity that, uh, fluctuates in price. And when the price goes up, it becomes really valuable to bad guys.
